extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters and writers preparing pitch/early development materials
extracted.subtask_description: Creating a beat sheet or beat board to outline the story beats for a film or TV script, using common story structures (Hero's Journey, three-act, Save the Cat) while balancing structure and inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story beat (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story beat is a smaller event that happens within a larger sequence or narrative; any moment that moves a story forward can be considered a beat, whether minor or major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats are the 'molecules' of a screenplay or television script. Each beat should seamlessly set up the next beat and push characters and narrative ahead. Example beats from Star Wars illustrate how each event drives the story forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat sheet (purpose and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat sheet is a document that outlines the story beats for a script you plan to write or have pitched and are developing; writers typically focus on major beats but may include minor beats depending on needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a beat sheet as a preliminary collection of ideas strung together chronologically to create a basic framework before creating an outline and script. Level of detail depends on whether you're working alone or sending materials to producers, and on personal preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat board (visual alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat board is a visual variation where writers jot beats on index cards or sticky notes and place them on a board or wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat boards allow quick reference and easy rearrangement of beats. Final Draft offers a virtual Beat Board that integrates with outlines and screenplays.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no single standard beat sheet format
rubrics_metrics.description: There really isn’t a standard beat sheet format; it comes down to what works best for the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need examples, follow established storytelling structures (Hero's Journey, Syd Field, Save the Cat), but adapt formats to your process and project requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero's Journey (high-level structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Joseph Campbell’s Hero’s Journey: three main stages — hero leaves ordinary world for adventure; faces challenges in new world(s); resolves ultimate challenge and is changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the basis for the three-act structure and commonly used in fantasy and adventure films (e.g., Star Wars). Use as a high-level scaffold for character arc and transformational beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act I — The Setup (Syd Field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act 1: The Setup — introduction of setting, characters, and main conflict; contains the inciting incident that forces the protagonist onto a new path and sets up Act 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish stakes and normal world; ensure the inciting incident clearly propels the protagonist into action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act II — The Confrontation (Syd Field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act 2: The Confrontation — a series of deepening conflicts and complications that build tension; should be the largest act and include the Midpoint and a 'lowest point' that leads into Act 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure Act 2 around escalating obstacles, a decisive midpoint turning point, and setup for a major setback that informs the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act III — The Resolution (Syd Field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act 3: The Resolution — contains the climax where the protagonist faces the main antagonist/conflict and reaches a final resolution, typically followed by an aftermath showing change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver a satisfying payoff to setup and confrontation, and show how the protagonist’s life has changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Opening Image
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening Image: A moment or image that sets the tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an evocative opening to establish mood and hint at the protagonist’s starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Theme Stated
rubrics_metrics.description: Theme Stated: Through dialogue or symbolism the story’s central theme is stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant thematic material early, often via another character's line, that the arc will test or fulfill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Set-up [1-10]
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-up [1-10]: Introduces the protagonist and their 'ordinary world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish who the protagonist is, their relationships, and what is at stake before the catalyst disrupts things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Catalyst
rubrics_metrics.description: Catalyst: An event or conflict that disrupts the protagonist’s world and sets the story in motion (a.k.a. the inciting incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the catalyst early to force the protagonist into a new situation that leads into the Debate and Act 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Debate [12-25]
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate [12-25]: The protagonist questions whether to deal with the primary conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this beat to show internal hesitation and stakes before the protagonist commits to Act 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Break Into Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Break Into Two: The protagonist finally accepts the call to action and leaves their ordinary world to enter a new and uncertain one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the transition into Act 2 — make the choice feel earned and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — B Story
rubrics_metrics.description: B Story: The introduction of a subplot, often a new character, that will help the protagonist to grow and learn new skills; often reflects the primary theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the B Story to provide emotional grounding and thematic reinforcement for the protagonist’s arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Fun and Games [30-55]
rubrics_metrics.description: Fun and Games [30-55]: The protagonist and supporting characters face the story’s main obstacles and challenges with a mix of success and failure; often contains 'trailer moments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver the premise’s promise and entertain while deepening stakes; this section showcases the central concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Midpoint: A major turning point where the stakes are raised after a false victory or defeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift the game — new information or stakes force characters into irreversible choices and escalate toward the 'bad guys close in.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Bad Guys Close In [55-75]
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad Guys Close In [55-75]: Things go further downhill for the protagonist as obstacles increase and 'fun and games' end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensify pressure and complications to propel the story toward the All Is Lost moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — All Is Lost [75]
rubrics_metrics.description: All Is Lost [75]: The protagonist hits rock bottom; it looks like all hope is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage a clear nadir that feels like utter defeat, setting up emotional reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Dark Night of the Soul [75-85]
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark Night of the Soul [75-85]: The protagonist reflects on their loss and what faces them if they continue facing the primary challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection and internal reckoning to prepare for the protagonist’s epiphany and plan forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Break Into Three [85]
rubrics_metrics.description: Break Into Three [85]: The protagonist has a realization or epiphany where they figure out how to overcome the obstacles (often by recalling something learned earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the solution feel rooted in earlier setup and character growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Finale [85-110]
rubrics_metrics.description: Finale [85-110]: The protagonist takes action based on their new awareness, faces their biggest obstacle and defeats the antagonist(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver an active, earned climax where skills/lessons from the B Story and earlier acts pay off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder 'Save the Cat' — Final Image [99-100]
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Image [99-100]: A concluding moment or image that mirrors the Opening Image but shows how the protagonist has grown and changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close with a resonant image that contrasts the opening and communicates transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner practical guidance — essential beats to include
rubrics_metrics.description: A beginner screenwriter should follow basic three-act structure and a few of the bigger and more essential beats cited by Blake Snyder (e.g. the Catalyst, Fun and Games, Midpoint, All is Lost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize major structural beats rather than trying to map every tiny moment; ensure the core turning points are strong and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-mapping / formulaic plotting (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping out every little moment beforehand can suck genuine inspiration from writing, resulting in a stock or formulaic script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers, agents and producers read many scripts and know standard beats; if your story follows beats too rigidly it may read as familiar or boring. Leave room for organic character reactions and surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-first beat construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal beat sheet should be just as focused on and constructed around character as the plot they're existing in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for 'the right story with the right character' — ensure beats arise from character choices and growth, not only from imposed structural obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the beat sheet as a flexible roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat sheet is a preliminary stage before creating an outline and script; once writing begins you should be prepared to rethink and modify your beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a healthy balance between outlining and inspiration: use the beat sheet as guidance, but allow for inspired detours and revisions during drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools and templates availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Draft and other tools offer structural templates (Save the Cat, Dan Harmon's Story Circle, The Writer's Journey, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available templates to learn structure or speed up organization, but customize to serve your story rather than slavishly following the template.
